turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Give me a second, the chart's only half loaded. Right. What has you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah it's nothing. I'm grand. Just a bit of a flutter, and my girlfriend made the appointment.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): A flutter. What does that feel like, in your own words?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The heart going a bit fast. Thumping. I'm not dying or anything.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? I clicked the wrong bit of the screen.

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The heart races, a thump in the chest, and it comes and goes. I haven't a clue when it started exactly, five-ish weeks maybe. Mostly at night, and before an exam or a meeting at work.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): And breathlessness, is that with it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A small bit short of breath when it happens. Nothing mad. I can still walk around grand.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it wake you out of sleep?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): My girlfriend says I'm restless at night. I notice the thumping when I'm trying to get to sleep, and then I'm grand in the morning, mostly.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain at all with these?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. It's not sore.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): You have exams and meetings. Are you stressed with them?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not a stressy person. Exams are exams. I'm grand with them.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you fainted, or come close to it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I haven't blacked out once.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Dizziness?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, the cursor's jumped. Dizzy or not dizzy?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not dizzy. I'm fine.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough, fever, any of that?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough and no fever. I'm not sick.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about coffee through the day?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A good bit, yeah. I do be on the coffee from early. Sure everyone drinks coffee.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many? Say it slow, I'm half reading an old letter here.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Four, well actually four or five mugs, sometimes six if the day's long. And a couple of energy drinks if there's a meeting.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six energy drinks? Is that every day?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, two. Two big cans, most days. I said a couple. It's not a big deal.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or is it a vape?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke cigarettes. I vape. It's only a vape.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long, and how much of the vape?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Two years, give or take. Through the day. I don't count the puffs.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): The odd pint at the weekend. Nothing wild.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the work, what is it you do?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Office job, accounts. I'm after starting the professional exams, so there's meetings and study on top. It's normal stuff.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Who's at home?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Just myself and the girlfriend. She booked this. I wouldn't have bothered, the parking was the worst part.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any medical conditions? Asthma, heart problems, thyroid?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. I'm healthy.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any operations?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Never had an operation.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines at the minute?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Not now. They gave me propranolol in the spring for the racing heart, and I stopped it in February, no, March.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Propranolol, what dose? Sorry, the screen jumped on me.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten milligram, I think. Once a day. I only took it a couple of weeks, it made me wrecked, so I stopped it in March.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was there anything else written up that you didn't take?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): The GP wrote a script for sertraline. I never took it. I didn't even collect it from the chemist.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No allergies.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): In the family, heart trouble or thyroid problems?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): My mam had an overactive thyroid years ago. Nobody with heart attacks, that I know of.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, let me read these off before the machine times out. Pulse is ninety-six, blood pressure one-eighteen over seventy-six, oxygen ninety-eight percent, and breathing sixteen.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbers are all right, but I still need to listen. Chest is clear, heart sounds are normal, the rhythm is regular just sitting here, and there's no swelling at the ankles.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): See? I'm grand. Can I head off?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not yet. My feeling is the coffee, the energy drinks and the vape are stirring the heart up, and the exams are a trigger even if you don't call it stress. I can't rule out a rhythm problem, or the thyroid, with your mam's history.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not the exams. And the vape is harmless. But do what you want.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm ordering an ECG today for the palpitations, and bloods for your thyroid, to check that's not driving it.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods as well? That's a lot for a flutter.

[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's the right check. When an episode starts, try slow breathing, in for four and out for six, for a few minutes. And cut the energy drinks right back, the coffee too if you can manage it.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Breathing exercises. I'll try them, I suppose. I'm not promising on the coffee.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in a fortnight and we'll go through the results. If you get chest pain, or you faint, don't wait on me, go to A&E.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

omissions.text: Palpitations were also described as a 'thump in the chest'.
The patient said the palpitations do not wake him from sleep; he notices the thumping when trying to get to sleep and is mostly fine in the morning.
Propranolol stop date is recorded incompletely: the patient said he stopped it in March after it made him feel 'wrecked'.
Previous prescription for sertraline was not taken and not collected from the pharmacy.
Family history was additionally negative for known heart attacks.

Doctor advised reducing vaping as part of likely triggers ('coffee, the energy drinks and the vape are stirring the heart up'), but the recorded counselling only includes cutting back energy drinks and coffee.
There was a real disagreement: the patient denied exams were a trigger/stress factor and said vaping was harmless, while the doctor felt exams and vaping were contributing.
